header:
The IRS Just Set
2027's Tax Numbers

lines.text: Your first $16,600 next year? Federal income tax-free.
lines.say: Your first sixteen thousand six hundred dollars next year? Federal income tax-free.

lines.text: That's the 2027 standard deduction for single filers, set Thursday by the IRS.
lines.say: That's the twenty twenty-seven standard deduction for single filers, set Thursday by the IRS.
It's up five hundred dollars from this year's sixteen thousand one hundred.

lines.text: Married and filing jointly? You get $33,200, up $1,000.
lines.say: Married and filing jointly? You get thirty-three thousand two hundred dollars, up a thousand.
Since twenty eighteen, it's climbed from twelve thousand dollars to sixteen thousand six hundred.

lines.text: The reason: inflation. Brackets rise an average of 3.2%, but rates stay the same.
lines.say: The reason: inflation. Brackets rise an average of three point two percent, but rates stay the same.

lines.text: For single filers, the 12% bracket will run to $52,025.
lines.say: For single filers, the twelve percent bracket will run to fifty-two thousand and twenty-five dollars.

lines.text: Our math: earn the same $60,000, and you'd owe about $68 less.
lines.say: Our math: earn the same sixty thousand dollars, and you'd owe about sixty-eight dollars less.

lines.text: One catch: this is for 2027 income, on the return you file in 2028.
lines.say: One catch: this is for twenty twenty-seven income, on the return you file in twenty twenty-eight.

lines.text: That's the money. Follow for more.
lines.say: That's the money. Follow for more.

post.title: The IRS just set 2027's tax-free amount: $16,600
post.ig:
Your first $16,600 next year? Federal income tax-free.
The IRS set the 2027 standard deduction on Nov 5: $16,600 for single filers (up $500) and $33,200 for married couples filing jointly (up $1,000).
Bracket thresholds rise an average of 3.2%; tax rates stay the same.
Our math: a single filer earning the same $60,000 owes about $68 less federal income tax.
It applies to 2027 income, on returns filed in 2028.
Sources: IRS (IR-2026-133, Rev. Proc. 2026-35), Journal of Accountancy, CPA Practice Advisor.
News and education, not financial advice.
